title: [CLO Master Express Lesson 15] Wedding Dress Teaching Live Broadcast (Part 2) Exquisite Wedding Dress Detail Making Tutorial
description:
How to create large-scale heavy industrial wedding dresses in CLO?  
Whether you have a girlish heart or you work in the fashion industry,  
you must be very interested!  
How do you make three-dimensional flowers and three-dimensional puffy tulle?  
This tutorial is just what you need!  
Here’s a little spoiler: the next live stream will be in mid-July, and the theme is very HOT~~
transcript:
Good evening everyone, I’m very happy to meet you all again here in the live broadcast room.  
Good evening everyone, I’m very happy to meet you all again here in the live broadcast room.  
My name is Evelyn, I am a 3D designer from Close Shanghai.  
Many students who followed our last live broadcast are already quite familiar with our wedding dress production.  
In the last session, we made the structure and sizing of our wedding dress.  
In this session, we will mainly focus on learning the production of details.  
Before we start, to save time, I have already enhanced the quality of our wedding dress.  
Next, first I will apply a saved pose that I prepared earlier.  
Here, I first tidy up my clothing.  
Deactivate my clothing.  
Then find the pose I saved.  
Change the pose accordingly.  
Next, I will ensure that the clothing still fits well after changing the pose.  
Here, if we want, we can delete the black texture on our shoes.  
Of course, this depends on everyone’s preference.  
At the same time, I can also turn off some display information,  
such as internal lines, base lines, the 3D pens we drew last time,  
and the display of our interfacing strips, etc.  
The first part we need to do is the pleating and piping section.  
When doing this step,  
first create the piping panel.  
When making pleats, the tool we need to use is the “pleat tool” in the cloth section.  
This pleat tool allows us to select any two points on the garment and adjust the fit of the clothing by pinching the fabric.  
From the tool’s description, it is clear that the pleat tool is suitable for adjusting the fit of the clothing.  
It is very suitable for pleating or creating volumetric details in 3D.  
Here, we proceed to make the pleats.  
First, click the starting point.  
Then click again at the ending point.  
After starting simulation, these two points will form a pinch pleat.  
Next, we use the edit pleat tool.  
Copy it.  
Copy it as a group.  
Then mirror paste it to create a complete group of pinch pleats.  
During this process, we can adjust its position  
to make the pleats look more regular.  
When pasting, right-click,  
enter the desired number of copies,  
and generate the full set of pleats.  
After generating, we may need to readjust the position.  
Here, I fine-tune the position.  
Once satisfied, we can copy the entire group out,  
completing the construction of the pleated panel.  
Next, since we want to make a sleeve panel,  
I used the edit arc tool on the hem,  
and the tool for generating smooth curves in the corners,  
to create a smooth arc.  
Before starting the simulation,  
it is very important that we first create the pleating effect,  
then apply it onto the garment.  
We use the fixed pin tool to place fixed pins at all four corners.  
Next, we can harden the panel before simulation.  
This helps form the shape.  
Also, reduce the particle distance;  
I set it to 8 here.  
This aims to better manifest the folds.  
At the same time, increase the pressure.  
I set it to 10 here.  
This applies an outward force on the panel, making it easier to form shape during simulation.  
After these operations, we can start the simulation.  
Let’s see the current shape.  
It is somewhat affected by hardening and the tension from the fixed pins, so it doesn’t form well yet.  
No worries, we remove the hardening.  
Now the panel floats upward.  
Since the pleating effect has appeared,  
we can release the pressure now.  
You can see the basic pleating trend has formed.  
We further adjust by reducing the particle distance.  
Now I set it to 5.  
The pleating ripple effect is now quite obvious.  
However, the detail still looks a bit stiff.  
Now, we reduce it to 3.  
It will warn that the simulation speed will slow down.  
Once simulation completes and the shape looks natural, we stop the simulation.  
Next, we arrange it.  
Those who watched last time will be more familiar.  
We arrange it as close as possible to the sewing position.  
I place it close.  
Since we want to make a sleeve,  
and the sleeve has a straight shoulder effect,  
we need to modify the panel.  
We modify it into a fan-shaped panel.  
At this point, some fake sewing pins on the edges may need repositioning.  
Then use the edit panel tool to modify the panel.  
After modification, we can add points and lines  
to locate where it needs to be sewn with the main rope.  
After locating, I find the corresponding position on the main rope.  
Here, I use a 1:2 or 2:1 ratio to find its position.  
When unsure, I use the positioning ball.  
Click in the 3D environment to find the position, then edit it in 2D.  
Using the small blue dots for positioning.  
Once done, adjust the position to be closer.  
Then we can sew it.  
Before sewing, since the main rope needs to participate in simulation,  
I change it from deactivated to frozen.  
Before simulation, I delete two fixed pins here.  
Then start the simulation.  
After simulation, I come to the front and use fixed pins.  
While simulation is active,  
let the panel naturally wrap around to the other end of the shoulder,  
wrapping around the arm.  
Then sew it.  
Similarly, delete the fixed pins and simulate again.  
Currently, the volume of the sleeve is quite large,  
different from the effect I want.  
No problem.  
I use the edit pleat tool again to tidy the pleat pins.  
Then reduce the sleeve panel length by about 3 cm.  
Now, this effect is what I’m satisfied with.  
I want to add lace to the pleated sleeve.  
First, I need to locate the sewing line for the lace.  
After using internal line spacing, I find the curve too large.  
I want it to be basically a straight line.  
So I use the edit curve point tool, select curve points, and delete them.  
Then, according to the length of this line, I construct the lace length.  
When constructing, first build a giant panel.  
Then use the well-known extend panel rotate tool to make the lace.  
After completion, it can be sewn very quickly.  
Then arrange it below.  
Currently, the particle distance is large,  
so I reduce the particle distance and simulate again.  
This lace effect is what I prefer.  
After this step, I want to add a pearl to every fabric gathering point on the pleats.  
Here, I use the button tool.  
First, I find the main rope,  
reactivate it,  
then find the button tool.  
Find a round button,  
adjust its width and thickness to be equal.  
This creates a pearl-like spherical button.  
After this, I can use the button tool to add, copy, and paste.  
Using the select-move button tool,  
copy and paste, and during pasting,  
input the number of buttonholes desired to automatically add evenly spaced pearl buttons.  
After finishing, I can quickly copy it to the lower position.  
At this point, the added buttons are just small spherical buttons.  
Don’t forget to add decorations on the lace as well.  
It will prompt that you can’t add decorations outside the panel on buttons.  
I will also give it a pearl-white color.  
After finishing, we can quickly align it to the other side.  
Did you notice anything?  
Is any information missing on the aligned version?  
When simulating, we can put parts that don’t need simulation back on the other side.  
After simulation, although we added buttons,  
our sewing needle hasn’t aligned to the other end.  
So we use the edit sewing tool,  
stick it to the other end.  
Once the position is found,  
we can re-simulate.  
Before starting simulation,  
to reduce conflict between button and sewing needle,  
I turned off conflict.  
After finishing, we complete the sleeve design on the other side.  
Re-activate it.  
We don’t need any extra panels.  
After that, we can start making the necklaces.  
After finishing the necklaces, we make the sleeves.  
The sleeves are now done.  
Next, we will make the pattern of the pattern.  
In our wedding dress design,  
we often encounter strong patterns,  
such as water patterns or necklace patterns.  
For example, when working on a car, we listen to other teachers.  
In this case, we can’t do a good job scanning parts.  
Therefore, I recommend when taking pictures,  
put the item on a background with strong color contrast.

After taking the photo, I paste the color in Photoshop.

chunks.title: [CLO Master Express Lesson 15] Wedding Dress Teaching Live Broadcast (Part 2) Exquisite Wedding Dress Detail Making Tutorial
chunks.content: ## Overview of Wedding Dress Detail Production and 3D Design Workflow This section introduces the focus on detailed production techniques for wedding dresses using CLO 3D software, including pose application, clothing adjustments, and preparation for detailed work such as pleating, piping, and accessory attachment. - The session primarily covers detailed garment construction following the structural and sizing work from the previous lesson. - Clothing pose is adjusted by applying saved poses and ensuring proper fit after transformation. - Display elements such as internal lines, interfacing strips, and drawn 3D pens can be toggled off to declutter the workspace. - Optional texture removal (e.g., black texture on shoes) can be done based on design preference. --- ## Pleating and Piping Techniques in CLO 3D This section details the creation of pleats and piping panels using CLO 3D's pleat tool, fixed pins, particle distance adjustments, and simulation settings to achieve realistic pleated fabric effects. - **Pleat Tool Usage:** - Select two points on the garment to create a pinch pleat during simulation. - Use the edit pleat tool to copy and mirror pleats for symmetry. - Right-click to enter the number of copies for repeated pleats. - Adjust pleat positions to maintain regularity. - **Panel Shaping:** - Use the edit arc tool and corner curve generation tools to create smooth sleeve panel edges. - Apply fixed pins at panel corners before simulation to maintain shape. - Harden the panel pre-simulation for structure support. - Particle distance settings control fold detail: - Start with 8 for basic folds - Reduce to 5 or 3 for finer pleat ripples (note: lower values slow simulation) - **Simulation Adjustments:** - Increase pressure (e.g., to 10) to apply outward force aiding shape formation. - Remove hardening if the panel shape is too stiff to allow natural fabric movement. - **Panel Modification for Sleeves:** - Modify pleated panels into fan shapes for sleeves with straight shoulder effect. - Reposition sewing points using the edit panel tool and 1:2 or 2:1 ratios. - Employ the positioning ball in 3D for precise alignment. - Sew panels to the main rope, switching its status from deactivated to frozen for simulation participation. - Use fixed pins during active simulation to guide natural wrapping of the sleeve panel. - Adjust sleeve volume by shortening panel length and refining pleat pins. --- ## Adding Lace and Decorative Elements to Sleeves This section explains how to add lace trims and pearl decorations to the pleated sleeves, including curve editing for lace placement and button tool usage for pearl creation. - **Lace Construction:** - Locate lace sewing line by adjusting internal line spacing. - Use edit curve point tool to simplify curves to near-straight lines. - Build lace length based on sewing line measurement. - Create a large panel and use the extend panel rotate tool to shape lace. - Reduce particle distance for finer lace simulation. - **Pearl Button Decoration:** - Use the button tool to create spherical buttons simulating pearls.

chunks.content: --- ## Adding Lace and Decorative Elements to Sleeves This section explains how to add lace trims and pearl decorations to the pleated sleeves, including curve editing for lace placement and button tool usage for pearl creation. - **Lace Construction:** - Locate lace sewing line by adjusting internal line spacing. - Use edit curve point tool to simplify curves to near-straight lines. - Build lace length based on sewing line measurement. - Create a large panel and use the extend panel rotate tool to shape lace. - Reduce particle distance for finer lace simulation. - **Pearl Button Decoration:** - Use the button tool to create spherical buttons simulating pearls. - Adjust button width and thickness equally for a pearl-like shape. - Copy and paste buttons evenly spaced along pleat gathering points. - Add pearl-white color to buttons for realism. - Align buttons and lace decorations symmetrically on both sleeves. - Use edit sewing tool to fix sewing needle alignment post-simulation. - Turn off conflict between buttons and sewing needles before final simulation. --- ## Applying Stickers and Textures for Patterned Details This section covers integrating strong pattern elements onto the wedding dress using sticker tools and Photoshop for texture preparation, focusing on water patterns and necklace motifs. - Take photos with high color contrast backgrounds (e.g., black or skin tone) for better scanning. - Use Photoshop to isolate and prepare sticker elements by removing background colors. - Apply stickers onto garment surfaces and adjust size and position via the sticker tool. - To create texture relief (unevenness), use calligraphy techniques with grayscale images: - White areas represent raised parts. - Black areas are flat. - Adjust particle diameter (e.g., 3mm) for detailed water-dye effects;
